summary: RW Aurigae is a young star about 509 light-years away that dims unpredictably behind clouds of dust. WANDERERS found no measurable motion between 2010 and 2026. Gaia lists only 0.03 arcseconds per year, too small to see. From September 2025 to September 2026 its brightness changed by +0.04 ± 0.08 magnitudes, which is within the uncertainty, so it looked steady. A few snapshots can still miss dimming that happens between them. Confidence is medium because the star is too bright for SPHEREx, and 188 of 199 measurements are flagged as saturated.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Gaia DR3 already lists this star, about 509 light-years away, and catalogues it as a variable, so it is known, not new. Across three SPHEREx visits from Sep 2025 to Sep 2026, its brightness changed by +0.04 ± 0.08 mag, which is smaller than the uncertainty, so it looked quiet. Caution: 188 of 199 measurements were saturated, so confidence is only medium. Dimming between snapshots could also be missed.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Mostly the saturation: 188 of 199 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because RW Aurigae is too bright, so its brightness comes from the star's faint outer glow. That uncertainty (0.08 mag) is about twice the change measured (0.04 mag). There were also only three visits, so a dimming between them could be missed. If other telescopes saw it dim during that year, "quiet" would be wrong.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE pictures from 2010 combined with SPHEREx images from 2025 and 2026 give a 16-year gap for spotting motion. Even so, RW Aurigae shifted only 0.37 arcseconds, too little to count as real motion. SPHEREx adds a spectrum across many wavelengths and repeat visits to check brightness. But this star is too bright for SPHEREx: 188 of its 199 measurements were flagged as saturated.
